subject: Creativity
title: Circular Design: Rethinking Waste as a Design Failure
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Circular Design: Rethinking Waste as a Design Failure.

hook.text: In nature, there's no such thing as waste. Every output is an input for something else.

buildup.text: The circular economy designs products to be reused, repaired, remanufactured, or recycled — eliminating the concept of.

discovery.text: Cradle to Cradle design creates two types of materials: biological (compostable) and technical (infinitely recyclable).

twist.text: Patagonia's 'Don't Buy This Jacket' campaign encouraged repair over replacement.

climax.text: The EU's Right to Repair legislation now requires electronics to be repairable for 10 years.

punchline.text: Waste isn't inevitable. It's a design choice. And we can choose differently.

quiz.question: What happened when Patagonia ran a 'Don't Buy This Jacket' campaign?

details.summary: Circular design treats waste as a design failure rather than an inevitable consequence. Products are designed from the start for disassembly, reuse, and recycling. The goal is to eliminate the concept of waste entirely by keeping materials in productive use indefinitely.
details.whyItMatters: The linear take-make-dispose model is environmentally unsustainable. Circular design offers a framework for creating products and systems that generate economic value without depleting finite resources.
takeaways: Waste is reframed as a failure of design rather than an inevitability
Products are designed for disassembly and material recovery from the start
Circular design aims to keep materials productive indefinitely

faq.question: How is circular design different from recycling?
faq.answer: Recycling addresses waste after it is created. Circular design prevents waste by designing products that can be fully disassembled, with components reused or materials recovered. The design intent eliminates the need for waste management entirely.

faq.question: Is circular design economically viable?
faq.answer: Increasingly yes. Companies like Patagonia, Interface, and Philips have demonstrated profitable circular models. Reducing material waste, extending product life, and selling services instead of products create new revenue streams while cutting costs.
